Jaou Tunis 2026 | From Idea to Image – Video Making

A look back at our hands-on video workshop with Momen Gharbi, where participants explored the different stages of video creation, from developing an idea to filming and editing their own short sequences.

A creative experience combining experimentation, storytelling and learning through practice.

📍 Quechlet El Attarine

جو تونس 2026 | من الفكرة إلى الصورة – ورشة في صناعة الفيديو

نعود معكم إلى أبرز لحظات ورشة صناعة الفيديو مع مؤمن الغربي، حيث تعرّف المشاركون على مختلف مراحل إنتاج الفيديو، انطلاقاً من تطوير الفكرة وصولاً إلى التصوير والمونتاج وإنجاز مقاطعهم الخاصة.

تجربة إبداعية جمعت بين التجربة وسرد القصص والتعلّم من خلال التطبيق.

Natasha Tontey 
​MACHO MYSTIC MELTDOWN Chapter 4: In A Muscle Mood 

Courtesy of the artist, Kamel Lazaar Foundation & Centre d’Art Contemporain Genève for BIM’26

Macho Mystic Meltdown Chapter 4: In a Muscle Mood brings together the Manguni Body Building Club of 1950s Jakarta and Sartana, a Minahasan street network formed in the early 1970s, known for its solidarity, protection of migrant communities, territorial power and reputation for violence.

The work explores the Manguni Club as a possible precursor to Sartana, where physical discipline, communal care and masculine identity intersect.
Set in a restaurant inspired by Jakarta’s Restaurant Trio, it stages an encounter between a Minahasan deserter and a Dutch-Javanese aristocrat, using food, wrestling, music, costume and sound to explore how trauma, power, intimacy and vulnerability pass across generations.

texte:
Jaou Tunis 2026 | Moving Images, Still Frames

A look back at our conversation with Lilia Ben Achour, film archivist and independent researcher, exploring the challenges of preserving and archiving Tunisia’s audiovisual heritage.

Through reflections and shared insights, the discussion opened up questions around how moving images are preserved, circulated and passed on across generations, highlighting the importance of safeguarding our audiovisual memory.

📍 Quechlet El Attarine
🗓️ 14 November

Part of Jaou Tunis 2026.

جو تونس 2026 | الصورة المتحركة، واللقطات الثابتة

نعود معكم إلى أبرز لحظات اللقاء مع ليليا بن عاشور، المتخصصة في أرشفة الأفلام والباحثة المستقلة، والذي تناول التحديات المرتبطة بحفظ وأرشفة التراث السمعي البصري التونسي.

من خلال النقاش وتبادل الأفكار، تطرّق اللقاء إلى طرق حفظ الصور المتحركة وتداولها ونقلها عبر الأجيال، مسلّطاً الضوء على أهمية الحفاظ على ذاكرتنا السمعية البصرية.

📍 قشلة العطّارين
🗓️ 14 نوفمبر

Leena Habiballa 
Unstrung, أحتاجُ دوزنة  2026 

single-channel video installation, 16 mm, black and white, digitised, 27’ 
Arabic with English subtitles 

Courtesy of the artist, Kamel Lazaar Foundation & Centre d’Art Contemporain Genève for BIM’26

Unstrung is a moving image work that attends to the affective economies of the Sudan war as they are articulated through registers of song, dance, music and poetry. 

Exploring the aesthetics of past and present Sudanese militarized cultures and their harnessing of revolutionary desires, the work unravels the ideological entanglements between sites of political violence and everyday mythmaking.  

In the work, analog 16mm printing techniques, performance, montage, and sonic interventions disrupt and repurpose archival material, footage, and sonic fragments, while deconstructing the social choreographies that sustain the life and memory of war within communities. 

By manipulating various militaristic and war archives against themselves, Unstrung attempts to articulate the appropriation of revolutionary energies through the cultural, affective, and embodied politics of war in Sudan.

Hajra Waheed 
A River Runs Beneath, 2026 
single-channel video installation, 14’48” 

A River Runs Beneath follows a village chief of a fishing community as he travels at night from the river towards the sea. Shot in one seemingly continuous take and unfolding in real time, the film follows his passage through darkness, guided by his own refrain. 

For generations, fishing communities have lived along these waters, with knowledge passed through direct transmission: observation, repetition, and embodied practice. 

The body is inseparable from the land, and from waters increasingly shaped by struggles over livelihood and access. To move through them is to carry memory into an uncertain present. 

The film’s slowness becomes a refusal of disappearance and acceleration. Time breaks to the rhythm of a low hum and the act of navigation. 

To remain with this passage is to remain with a place under pressure, and with what it carries. There is no resolution, only duration. A quiet insistence against erasure.
